summary:
No trans-specific statute, enforcement series or incident is documented for Yozgat province. The absence of a local record does not indicate local safety: Yozgat stands under the national framework of Turkey, and the rules below reach the province unchanged.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked omnibus draft, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the Turkish penal code to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" with up to three years in prison, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. The draft had not been passed when reported.

The same package would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care, including surgery, from 18 to 25, conditioned on mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, patients up to three years with possible pretrial detention. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft. Human Rights Watch warned that the measure would force treatment underground and leave LGBT people in constant fear of arrest.

Kaos GL's 2025 review, "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People", finds that hostility toward LGBTI+ people became explicit state policy. Instructions issued to public institutions under a family-protection banner were accompanied by the closure of an LGBTI+ rights organisation for the first time in years, restrictions on expression and artistic freedom, and events cancelled or banned.

The review counts 313 liberty violations in 2025, about two and a half times the previous year, alongside 299 detention decisions. Torture and ill-treatment violations rose from 51 to 89. It records 61 travel bans, and private-life violations rising from 16 to 67, among them obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy.

Six right-to-life violations were recorded in 2025, including three hate-motivated killings, with trans people identified as the most affected group.
tangentialFactors:
The distinction between pending law and applied law has narrowed. The draft package reported in October 2025 was not enacted, yet monitoring across Turkey through 2025 recorded detention decisions, event bans and interference with private life at a volume consistent with authorities acting ahead of legislation. A visitor in Yozgat should expect the conduct of enforcement rather than the text of the statute to set the practical boundary.

Documentary checks are the standard occasion for such encounters. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. Every stop is therefore an occasion on which a passport can be compared against presentation, in Yozgat as in Istanbul.

The escalation is measurable year over year: liberty violations roughly two and a half times the 2024 count, torture and ill-treatment up from 51 to 89, private-life violations up from 16 to 67. This is a nationwide trend rather than a cluster around one city.

No sub-national breakdown accompanies the 2025 monitoring figures, so Yozgat cannot be distinguished from other provinces on the basis of the available counts. Treat the national pattern as the floor of expectation for the province.
localsOnly:
Residents face interference with transition care directly. Obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy is recorded among the private-life violations that rose from 16 to 67 during 2025, and the draft package would set the floor for gender-affirming care at 25 years of age, with mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals.

Penalties under the pending package fall on providers as well as patients: fines and up to seven years of imprisonment for healthcare professionals performing gender-affirming interventions, up to three years for patients, with pretrial detention available.

Organised LGBTI+ life is constrained by administrative action. Kaos GL records one LGBTI+ rights organisation closed during 2025, the first such closure in years, alongside restrictions on expression and artistic freedom and the cancellation or banning of events.

Movement and bodily integrity are also affected. The 2025 counts include 61 travel bans and 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51 the year before, within a total of 313 liberty violations and 299 detention decisions.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 11th Judicial Package has been enacted since the Human Rights Watch report of 29 October 2025 is unresolved in available sources. The draft's current legislative status should be verified against newer reporting before it is treated as either law or abandoned.

No source establishes whether the Kaos GL 2025 counts include any case arising in Yozgat province. The province's contribution to the national totals is not sourced.

Data on Yozgat-specific police practice, hospital boards, detention facilities or local support organisations was not located. Nothing in the inventory confirms or excludes such provision in the province.

Whether any of the 61 travel bans, 299 detention decisions or six right-to-life violations recorded in 2025 involved residents of Yozgat is not sourced.
